candidate_payload.early_body_text: liosis. surgical cor- rection was impossible as he was no longer fit for surgery. late referral of this patient resulted in a poor quality of life which would have been avoidable by earlier referral. intravenous methocarbamol in the treatment of stiff-man syndrome stiff-man syndrome is a rare disorder recognized by continuous progressive rigidity with superimposed pain- ful, intermittent muscle spasms." the axial and lower extremity muscles are most involved. during severe spasms, the limbs are usually held in distorted postures and the patient may become immobilized.2~3~i these spasms can be provoked by sensory stimuli, but disap- pear during sleep, general anesthesia, and following neuromuscular blockade. emg demonstrates a sus- tained interference pattern reflecting continuous motor unit activity3.'; the spasms are not due to cramps, con- tractures, or myokymia. the etiology of this disorder is unknown. it probably results from decreased gamma-aminobutyric acid (gaba) activity, or increased catecholamine activity in the central nervous system. an autoimmune basis is sug- gested by the association with other autoimmune disor- ders, the presence of other organ-specific serum au- toantibodies, and the presence of antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase in 60% of patients' serum and csf.' effective, though limited, forms of treatment include diazepam, baclofen, clonazepam, and sodium val- pr~ate.~.~ rapid resolution of spasms in a patient follow- ing intravenous methocarbamol (robaxinr) prompted this report. a 41-year-old man developed, over the past 18 months, progressive low back and bilateral leg stiffness 434 letters to the editor muscle & nerve april 1993 10974598, 1993, 4, downloaded from https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/mus.880160415 by university of calgary, wiley online library on [08/06/2023]. see the terms and conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on wiley online library for rules of use; oa articles are governed by the applicable creative commons license with superimposed episodes of painful and disabling spasms. they were precipitated by manipulation and re- solved during sleep. he had been treated with combina- tions of various analgesics. his past medical history is otherwise unremarkable. immediately following a lumbar facetal block for low back pain, he developed spasms of both legs and lower paravertebral muscles with opisthotonus. his hips and knees were extended and the ankles inverted and plan- tar-flexed in a forceful, fixed posture. sodium pentothal anesthesia terminated the spasms on two occasions. emg showed continuous activity of normal motor units. he was treated with 150 mg of intravenous diazepam in 2 days, and 60 mg of oral baclofen daily with minimal effect. one gram of methocarbamol was then adminis- tered intravenously over 1 hour and resulted in imme- diate resolution of his spasms with significant improve- ment of muscle rigidity lasting a few hours. he had mild headache and lethargy following the infusion. he was maintained on a combination of oral baclofen, diaze- pam, and methocarbamol. neurological examination after improvement showed paraspinal and lower extremity muscle rigidity, marked hyperlordosis, and difficulty walking due to se- vere stiffness. the rest of his exam was normal. the following tests were normal: mri of the thoracic and lumbar spine; serum calcium, magnesium, potassium, and sodium; creatine kinase; glucose tolerance test; urine myoglobin; antinuclear and antimicrosomal anti- bodies; antibodies to gastric parietal cells, islet cells, and thyroglobulin; and ischemic forearm exercise test. im- munostaining of the patient’s serum did not detect an- tibodies against rat cerebellar neurons. our patient fulfilled the criteria of stiff-man syn- drome.*,’ methocarbamol, a derivative of mephenesin carbamate, is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant whose precise mechanism of action is unknown. it may have some effect on central gaba systems or entirely different effects elsewhere. it has no direct effect on skeletal muscle, neuronal conduction, or neuromuscular transmission. it has been utilized in the management of tetanus, but is ineffective for the treatment of chronic spasticity and dyskinesias. ls4 given the usual difficulty in treating painful spasms and the rapid relief in our patient, we suggest that in- travenous methocarbamol be considered in the treat- ment of stiff-man syndrome. we are grateful to dr. solimena for performing the immuno- staining studies and bobbi phelps for typing the manuscript. james m. voci, md mazen al-hakim, md yoni dokko, md m. bashar katirjl, md department of neurology case western reserve university university hospitals of cle
